The bones of a very good VS-like are absolutely here. Also getting definite Zombies Ate My Neighbors vibes, and that is high praise. Can I recommend it? Sort of. I guess what I'm saying is you should definitely pick this up for what it looks like it's going to be in the future, but what it is today won't last you more than a few hours as there's no real motivation to progress/replay, It's really missing that core roguelike/lite progression loop of unlocks and stuff. Like, yeah, you unlock a few characters, but just a few. You unlock a few new gadgets, but just a few. So there's very little incentive to keep pushing up a map that doesn't appear to end (currently, anyway.) The camp system seems like there will be a lot more going on eventually, but right now it's pretty thin. There's also a separate minigame component that looks like the zombie papers please trend that lets you trade away excess gear, but I only tried it once in my 4 or so hours with the game, and it wasn't super engaging.

Dead Engine is a demanding and systems-driven survival experience that blends fast-paced action with long-term decision-making in a bleak, pixel-art apocalypse. Developed by Chocolate Dungeon Games and published by Red Axe Games, the game positions itself as a tense balance between moment-to-moment combat and the slow, fragile construction of safety in a city that actively resists being reclaimed. From the outset, it’s clear that Dead Engine isn’t interested in power fantasy; it’s about endurance, improvisation, and the compounding consequences of small choices. The core loop revolves around venturing out from a fragile base into procedurally structured city districts filled with resources, threats, and hard decisions. Exploration is inherently risky, as enemies are not static obstacles but adaptive forces that respond to your presence. Zombies move in groups, funnel through chokepoints, and escalate pressure when engagements drag on. Combat is responsive and lethal on both sides, encouraging players to think tactically about positioning, terrain, and escape routes rather than charging headlong into every encounter. The constant tension between looting just a little more and knowing when to retreat gives each run a sharp edge. Inventory management is a defining pillar of the experience. Everything you carry lives in a limited backpack that must be carefully organized, expanded, and optimized. Items can be combined or rearranged to conserve space, turning inventory into a puzzle under pressure. This system elevates looting from a simple grab-and-go activity into a strategic layer that influences survival odds. Deciding whether to carry extra ammo, crafting materials, or medical supplies often determines whether a run ends in success or collapse, and the game rarely offers forgiving margins for error. Beyond individual runs, Dead Engine introduces a surprisingly deep camp management layer. Survivors encountered in the field can be recruited, traded with, or ignored, and each decision carries risk. Bringing someone back to camp may strengthen your group, but it can also introduce hidden dangers, including infection or morale problems. Camp resources like food, shelter quality, and hygiene must be maintained to prevent decline, turning the base into a living system rather than a static checkpoint. These mechanics give weight to downtime between expeditions and reinforce the idea that survival is collective, not solitary. Trading and interaction further flesh out the world. Encounters with other survivors often unfold through brief exchanges that hint at personal histories and shared desperation. These moments add narrative texture without relying on lengthy exposition, allowing emergent stories to form naturally. A trade gone wrong or a missed opportunity can linger across multiple runs, shaping how players approach future encounters and reinforcing the game’s bleak tone. Visually, Dead Engine embraces gritty pixel art that prioritizes readability and atmosphere over ornamentation. Environments are dense with detail, from crumbling interiors to claustrophobic alleys that double as tactical spaces. The art style supports gameplay by clearly defining hazards, cover, and enemy movement, while also selling the oppressive mood of a city in decay. Environmental traps and destructible elements allow players to manipulate terrain to their advantage, adding another layer of strategy to combat and escape. As an Early Access title, Dead Engine shows both ambition and roughness. Its systems are already interlocked in compelling ways, but balance and polish are ongoing concerns. Some mechanics can feel opaque at first, and certain runs may hinge on luck as much as skill. However, the foundation is strong, and updates have focused on expanding locations, refining progression paths, and clarifying risk–reward choices. The sense that the game is evolving alongside its community fits well with its themes of adaptation and survival. Ultimately, Dead Engine stands out for its refusal to simplify survival. It asks players to juggle action, logistics, and human consequences simultaneously, and it rarely cushions failure. For those who enjoy roguelites that generate tension through systemic pressure rather than spectacle, it offers a rich and often punishing experience. While still in the process of refinement, it already delivers a distinctive blend of tactical combat, inventory strategy, and camp-level storytelling that makes each run feel hard-earned and memorable. Rating: 6/10

和5个月前相比，机制、数值都改动很多，但核心内容依旧给人一种粗制滥造的感觉。 还是那句老话，比起搜打撤，玩法更类似于吸血鬼幸存者+背包英雄的肉鸽游戏，但又完全比不过两者的魅力。虽然有局外成长和物资积累，但重玩价值并不高，体验依旧一般 -------------------------------------------- 2026.01.26 游戏目前完成度很低了，比如UI文字太小，物品只能在战斗中合成却不能在营地合成，音效不全等等。 比起搜打撤，玩法更类似于吸血鬼幸存者+背包英雄（所谓的搜刮物资，搜的全是战斗技能和被动技能，类似目前的一些背包格子类肉鸽手游）。

I really loved the concept, it’s very fun. The art is beautiful, and the survival gameplay is enjoyable. It has some issues, but since it’s released in early access, I believe they’ll sort them out. It will get better as it receives updates. I hope gamepad support arrives very soon.

The game already has a lot of content despite being in early access. In my opinion, it’s in a very good state. Compared to day one, they’ve clearly worked on balance and are continuing to improve it. I’m really excited for the full release — it feels like something amazing is coming. Reserve your spot now.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Dead Engine is far better and more polished than I expected! The game delivers a post-apocalyptic zombie theme in a very strategic and dynamic way. The hand-crafted pixel art looks fantastic and does a great job setting the atmosphere, while the gameplay keeps you constantly engaged. What really stands out: The inventory and backpack management system is creative and very satisfying to use Zombies aren’t just mindless enemies; their behavior forces you to think and play strategically Camp management, trading events, and discovering survivors’ stories add real depth to the experience Every run feels different, which makes the game highly replayable. You can clearly see the care put into both the design and the balance. On top of that, the developers seem genuinely invested in improving the game and listening to community feedback, which is always a huge plus. Highly recommended. If you enjoy roguelike and survival games, Dead Engine is absolutely worth your time.

The bag mechanics and the survivor camp mechanics are a fresh take on the genre and i feel like these mechanics should be the basis of the game moving forward. However I do agree with most comments that the map and trade mechanics feel rather pointless and unpolished. Additionally a lack of controller support was a negative for me but that's a personal point. I see decent potential in the game as long as the devs focus more on the casual roguelike experience over the trade and map mechanics. Overall it's a fun time with great potential.

Dead Engine delivers a smooth and focused gameplay experience. The mechanics are simple but effective, without unnecessary complexity. Progression feels satisfying, and the game maintains a consistent pace throughout. A clean and enjoyable experience for players who appreciate its genre.

It's not bad, per se, but I really don't feel like it brings anything in particular. If: A. If you haven't ever played a game like Vampire Survivors: You should probably start with the original, or one of the more expansive, bigger budget clones. B. If you've played a bunch of Vampire Survivor-likes, I don't think this one is going to bring you anything fresh or exciting. In two hours I managed just over two runs, winning both times on the highest difficulty available, and I'm not particularly good at these. The game boasts an "item fusion system" but it's just a very linear upgrade system that doesn't really add anything in practice. You walk up to a chest, see it has a Level 2 Boot, and add it to your inventory if you have room. If you already have a Level 2 Boot specifically, you may stack them into a Level 3 Boot. But in another game, you would simply find the level 3 boot, equip it, and trash the level 2 boot for space. Or find a +1 Bootfulness potion to go from 2 to 3. I can imagine scenarios where item fusion might create interesting gameplay spaces (if you had, for example, a party in a strategy game, deciding whether to try to give everyone a gun or consolidate your guns into one designated Good Gun and let everyone else play support.) But as it is you're just wandering around opening chests and watching the numbers go up and the colors change.
